title: Bright Lines: How to Use Interleaving Effectively
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick opens a series on applying learning-science findings in real classrooms, warning that the 'science of learning' risks becoming another failed fad if it is applied as a menu of strategies rather than a set of principles. He argues that the field lacks 'bright lines' for effective, scalable implementation and that strategies such as interleaving depend on task, content and prior knowledge. Using Jeri Little and colleagues' recent experiments, he shows that interleaving benefits learners who memorise examples, while learners who abstract rules do better with blocked practice. He translates this into worked classroom sequences for distinguishing quadratic from linear equations and for Spanish verb conjugation. The piece closes with conditions for using interleaving, when to avoid it, and adjustments for students with low prior knowledge and for advanced students, recommending hybrid blocked-then-interleaved sequences.
points: Hendrick warns that evidence-based teaching reduced to checklists ('interleave, retrieve, space, elaborate') ignores how strategies interact and for whom they work.
Little and colleagues found that memorisers learn better from interleaved examples while rule-abstractors learn better from blocked examples, so the best sequence depends on how the student thinks.
In the Spanish example, blocking reveals the internal consistency of -ar endings while interleaving mimics the real-world need to select the right rule.
Interleaving is most useful when concepts are easily confused and learners have adequate prior knowledge, and should be avoided when introducing new concepts or with learners lacking basics.
For low-prior-knowledge students he recommends starting blocked and moving to interleaving, with extra scaffolding and explicit feature highlighting.
quotes: Interleaving, on the other hand, mimics the real-world challenge of having to select the right conjugation rule based on a verb’s ending. It encourages learners to become fluent at spotting patterns and switching rules.

Too often, evidence-based teaching is reduced to checklists: interleave, retrieve, space, elaborate etc. without considering how they interact and how they might determine long-term learning. Their effectiveness depends on the task, the content, and crucially, the learner’s prior knowledge.
Memorisers did better when examples were interleaved. They relied on surface similarity, and seeing examples from different categories helped them learn to discriminate.

Those who approach tasks by memorising examples perform better when materials are interleaved. But learners who try to abstract rules perform better when examples are blocked by category. In short, the optimal study sequence depends not just on the task, but on the to-be-learned material and as a result, how the student thinks.

This has direct implications for education. Teachers should therefore consider not just what they teach, but how students are likely to learn. One-size-fits-all activities (even well-supported ones like interleaving) may miss the mark if they are not considered in the broader trajectory of student learning.

Blocking gives students a chance to notice the internal consistency within a verb group. They can see that all -ar verbs follow the same endings — o, as, a, amos, áis, an — without the distraction of competing patterns.

The takeaway is not to use interleaving as an activity or strategy, but to be more precise about when and for whom it works and to view it as one lever in a broader ecosystem of learning. If the goal is to help students spot subtle differences (e.g., in art history or diagnosis), interleaving may help. But if they need to extract an underlying principle (e.g., grammar rules or physics laws), some initial blocking might serve them better.
